entries.meaning: In a sudden, unpleasant way that clashes with what is around it. ---
examples: The ending felt jarringly different from the rest of the movie.
The alarm went off jarringly at 5 a.m.
A jarringly bright sign stood next to the old church.
entries.type: degree — before an adjective; also manner
entries.position: before its word — usually an adjective (jarringly different)

entries.meaning: In a cheerful, lively and confident way. ---
examples: He walked jauntily down the street, whistling.
She wore her hat tilted jauntily to one side.
The little dog trotted jauntily beside its owner.
entries.modifies: verbs, especially of walking and wearing

entries.meaning: Jealously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He watched jealously as she danced with someone else.
The other kids looked jealously at his new bike.
The recipe is a jealously guarded family secret.
The two agencies jealously protect their budgets.

senses.head: With jealousy or envy
examples: He watched jealously as she danced with someone else.
The other kids looked jealously at his new bike.

senses.head: Very carefully, so as not to lose or share something
examples: The recipe is a jealously guarded family secret.
The two agencies jealously protect their budgets.

entries.position: end — also before a participle (jealously guarded)

entries.meaning: With sudden, uneven starts and stops. ---
examples: The old elevator moved jerkily up to the tenth floor.
The video played jerkily on my slow connection.
He was learning to drive a stick shift, so the car moved jerkily.

entries.meaning: Together, shared by two or more people or groups. ---
examples: The house is jointly owned by the two sisters.
The event was organized jointly by the city and the university.
Married couples can file their taxes jointly.
entries.position: end — also mid or before a participle (jointly owned)

entries.meaning: As a joke; not seriously. ---
examples: "Don't be late or you're fired," she said jokingly.
We jokingly call our tiny kitchen "the office."
He jokingly suggested we skip work and go to the beach.

entries.meaning: In a friendly, cheerful and good-humored way. ---
examples: The old man greeted us jovially at the door.
"Come on in, the water's fine!" he called jovially.
They chatted jovially over a few beers.

entries.meaning: With great happiness. ---
examples: The kids ran joyfully into the waves.
The church bells rang joyfully after the wedding.
She joyfully announced that she was pregnant.

entries.meaning: With great, open happiness; a slightly more literary word than joyfully. ---
examples: The crowd sang joyously as the team paraded through town.
The dogs barked joyously when we got home.
The holiday was celebrated joyously in every neighborhood.

entries.meaning: With great joy, especially after a success or victory. ---
examples: Fans cheered jubilantly as the final whistle blew.
"We did it!" she shouted jubilantly.
The players hugged jubilantly on the field.

entries.meaning: By a court or judge, or in a way that concerns the courts. ---
examples: The settlement must be judicially approved before it takes effect.
The right to privacy has been judicially recognized for decades.
When the two sides couldn't agree, the dispute was settled judicially.
entries.type: manner — by or through a court
entries.position: end — also before a participle (judicially approved)
entries.contrast: Not judiciously 'with good judgment': judicially is about courts and judges.

entries.meaning: With good judgment and care, especially in using something limited. ---
examples: Use the hot sauce judiciously — it's very strong.
The school spent its small budget judiciously.
She chose her words judiciously during the interview.
entries.contrast: Not judicially 'by a court': judiciously means 'with good judgment'. Russian юридически is legally or judicially, never judiciously.

entries.meaning: Almost; very nearly. ---
examples: I'm just about ready — give me two minutes.
Just about everyone was there.
We've tried just about everything.
entries.modifies: adjectives, verbs, and words like everyone, everything, all
entries.contrast: Just about to + verb is different: about to means вот-вот, and just strengthens it (The movie is just about to start).

entries.meaning: As a precaution, because something might happen. ---
examples: Take an umbrella, just in case.
I made extra food just in case.
Write down my number, just in case.
entries.contrast: At the end of a clause it is an adverb (Take an umbrella, just in case). Followed by a clause it is a conjunction (Take an umbrella just in case it rains = на случай, если). It is not if: in case it rains means as a precaution against rain, not on condition that it rains.

entries.meaning: Only a moment before it would have been too late. ---
examples: We got to the gate just in time.
The ambulance arrived just in time.
She finished the slides just in time for the meeting.
entries.русский: как раз вовремя, в последний момент
entries.contrast: In time means early enough (in time for dinner); on time means at the scheduled time, not late (the train left on time). Just in time is the close call.

entries.meaning: Just now has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Who was that on the phone just now?
I saw her in the hallway just now.
What did you say just now?
I'm busy just now — can I call you back?
She's not in the office just now.

senses.head: A moment ago
examples: Who was that on the phone just now?
I saw her in the hallway just now.
What did you say just now?

senses.head: At this moment; right now
examples: I'm busy just now — can I call you back?
She's not in the office just now.

entries.contrast: In American English just now usually means a moment ago and takes the simple past (I saw him just now, not I have seen him just now). For the present Americans more often say right now.

entries.meaning: At exactly that moment, often when something unexpected happened. ---
examples: I was about to leave, and just then the phone rang.
Just then, the lights went out.
She walked in just then and heard everything.
entries.русский: в этот самый момент, как раз тогда
entries.type: time — at that exact moment in a past story
entries.modifies: a whole clause, usually in the past tense
entries.contrast: Just then points to a moment in a story (в этот момент); just now usually means a moment ago, measured from the present (только что).

entries.meaning: For a good reason; in a way that is fair and reasonable. ---
examples: Her parents are justifiably proud of her.
Customers were justifiably angry about the delays.
Justifiably or not, he felt he'd been treated unfairly.
entries.type: stance — the speaker agrees the feeling or action is reasonable
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (justifiably proud); front with a comma

entries.meaning: Strongly and sharply, in feeling, awareness or interest. ---
examples: She was keenly aware that everyone was watching her.
His absence was keenly felt at the reunion.
Fans are keenly awaiting the band's new album.
entries.type: degree — with aware, felt, interested; also manner
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or participle (keenly aware); end after a verb

entries.meaning: Somewhat; a little; in a way. ---
examples: I'm kind of tired — can we go home?
The movie was kind of boring.
I kind of hoped you'd call.
entries.form: the noun kind + of, fused; often spelled kinda in casual writing
entries.contrast: It is an adverb only before a verb, adjective or adverb (I'm kind of tired). Before a noun it is the noun kind + of (What kind of car? = какая машина). Sort of works the same way.

entries.meaning: Informal for kind of: somewhat, a little. ---
examples: I'm kinda tired, so I'll stay home tonight.
That movie was kinda weird.
I kinda like him, to be honest.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective, adverb or verb
entries.contrast: Kinda is how kind of sounds in fast speech. It is fine in texts and casual writing but not in essays, reports or business email — write kind of, somewhat or a little there.

entries.meaning: Kindly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A neighbor kindly offered to water our plants.
She smiled kindly at the nervous boy.
He doesn't take kindly to being told what to do.
Kindly return the form by Friday.
Would you kindly stop kicking my seat?

senses.head: In a kind, generous or friendly way
examples: A neighbor kindly offered to water our plants.
She smiled kindly at the nervous boy.
He doesn't take kindly to being told what to do.

senses.head: Please; used in formal or annoyed requests
examples: Kindly return the form by Friday.
Would you kindly stop kicking my seat?

entries.type: manner; also a formal request marker (Kindly reply by Friday)
entries.position: end — in the manner sense; mid before the verb in requests and kindly offered
entries.form: -ly from kind; also an adjective (a kindly old man)
entries.contrast: Kindly is also an adjective (a kindly face). Not take kindly to means 'dislike': He doesn't take kindly to criticism. Kindly in requests sounds formal or irritated in American English — please is the everyday word.

entries.meaning: Knowingly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He knowingly sold a car with bad brakes.
I would never knowingly lie to you.
It is a crime to knowingly make a false statement to the police.
She smiled knowingly when I mentioned his name.
The two friends looked at each other knowingly.

senses.head: Deliberately, while knowing the facts
examples: He knowingly sold a car with bad brakes.
I would never knowingly lie to you.
It is a crime to knowingly make a false statement to the police.

senses.head: In a way that shows you understand something secret or not said
examples: She smiled knowingly when I mentioned his name.
The two friends looked at each other knowingly.

entries.position: mid — for 'deliberately'; end in the 'understanding' sense (smiled knowingly)

entries.meaning: With a lot of slow, hard effort. ---
examples: He laboriously copied every page by hand.
The truck climbed laboriously up the mountain road.
She spelled out each word laboriously.

entries.meaning: Without energy, care or enthusiasm. ---
examples: The team played lackadaisically in the first half.
He did his chores lackadaisically, missing half the dishes.
The waiter wandered lackadaisically over to our table.

entries.meaning: Using very few words. ---
examples: "Nope," the rancher replied laconically.
He described the accident laconically, as if it were nothing.
She answered every question laconically.

entries.meaning: In a weak, unconvincing way. ---
examples: "The dog ate my homework," he said lamely.
She apologized lamely and changed the subject.
The movie ends lamely, with no real payoff.

entries.meaning: To a disappointing or regrettable degree; also, used to say a fact is regrettable. ---
examples: Public transportation in the city is lamentably slow.
Lamentably few voters showed up for the primary.
Lamentably, the old theater was torn down in the 1970s.
entries.type: degree — formal, before an adjective; also stance
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or few (lamentably slow); front with a comma as a stance adverb

entries.meaning: Slowly and with little energy, often in a relaxed way. ---
examples: The cat stretched languidly in the sun.
A ceiling fan turned languidly overhead.
She waved languidly from the hammock.

entries.meaning: In a big, important or noticeable way; in loom large and live large. ---
examples: The deadline loomed large over the whole team.
As the election got closer, the economy loomed larger in voters' minds.
After the lottery win, they started living large.
entries.русский: крупно, во весь рост; на широкую ногу
entries.type: manner — only in set phrases (loom large, live large)
entries.modifies: a few verbs: loom, figure, live, write
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective large
entries.contrast: Large is almost always an adjective (a large house). As an adverb it lives only in set phrases; by and large 'generally' and at large 'not caught' are fixed phrases with their own meanings.

entries.meaning: Mentioned last, but just as important as the others. ---
examples: Last but not least, I want to thank my parents.
And last but not least, our drummer, Kevin!
Bring sunscreen, water and, last but not least, your ticket.
entries.русский: последний по порядку, но не по значению
entries.type: linking — introducing the final item in a list
entries.modifies: a whole clause or the last item in a list

entries.meaning: At a later time; afterward. ---
examples: I'll explain it to you later on.
Later on, she moved to Chicago.
We'll deal with that problem later on in the course.
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause

entries.meaning: Sideways; or, in a job, to a position at the same level. ---
examples: The crab moved laterally across the sand.
Instead of a promotion, she moved laterally to the marketing team.
The quarterback threw the ball laterally to the running back.
entries.contrast: Move laterally in a company means to change jobs at the same level, not to be promoted. Think laterally is mostly British; Americans say think outside the box.

entries.meaning: So much that it is ridiculous. ---
examples: The special effects in that movie are laughably bad.
They offered me a laughably small raise.
His excuse was laughably thin.

entries.meaning: Laughingly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: "You're hopeless," she said laughingly.
He laughingly admitted he had no idea how to cook.
We stayed in what was laughingly called a luxury hotel.
The closet I work in is laughingly referred to as an office.

senses.head: While laughing, or in a joking way
examples: "You're hopeless," she said laughingly.
He laughingly admitted he had no idea how to cook.

senses.head: Ironically; used when the name given to something is far from the truth
examples: We stayed in what was laughingly called a luxury hotel.
The closet I work in is laughingly referred to as an office.

entries.position: end — for 'with a laugh'; mid before a participle in the ironic sense (laughingly called)

entries.meaning: In a generous, rich or expensive way. ---
examples: The hotel lobby was lavishly decorated with marble and gold.
They entertained lavishly at their beach house.
The book is lavishly illustrated with color photos.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (lavishly decorated)

entries.meaning: In a way that is allowed by law. ---
examples: Only people who are lawfully present can apply for the program.
Do you take this woman to be your lawfully wedded wife?
The officer said the search was conducted lawfully.
entries.position: end — also before a participle (lawfully married)

entries.meaning: Slowly and without much effort, often in a relaxed way. ---
examples: We spent Sunday morning lying lazily in bed.
The river wound lazily through the valley.
The essay was lazily written, with no real research.

entries.meaning: Especially not; less than anyone or anything else. ---
examples: Nobody was happy with the result, least of all the coach.
I don't want to hurt anyone, least of all you.
No one expected her to win, least of all herself.
entries.русский: меньше всего, и уж точно не
entries.type: focusing — after a negative, picking out the least likely case
entries.position: after its word — after the negative statement, before the person or thing picked out
entries.modifies: a noun phrase added to a negative statement

entries.meaning: Clearly enough to be read. ---
examples: Please print your name legibly.
My doctor doesn't write very legibly.
Try to write more legibly on the exam.

entries.meaning: Legitimately has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The president was legitimately elected.
The money was earned legitimately.
Can I legitimately deduct my home office?
You can legitimately ask why the project took so long.
Fans could legitimately complain about the ticket prices.

senses.head: According to the law or the rules
examples: The president was legitimately elected.
The money was earned legitimately.
Can I legitimately deduct my home office?

senses.head: With good reason; fairly
examples: You can legitimately ask why the project took so long.
Fans could legitimately complain about the ticket prices.

entries.type: manner; also stance (you can legitimately ask)
entries.position: end — for 'legally'; mid in the 'reasonably' sense
entries.contrast: In informal American speech legitimately (and slang legit) also means 'really, truly': I was legitimately scared.

entries.meaning: Slowly and in a relaxed way, without hurrying. ---
examples: The boat drifted leisurely down the river.
They strolled leisurely through the park after lunch.
We ate leisurely on the porch and watched the sun go down.
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective leisurely
entries.contrast: leisurely already ends in -ly, so one form serves as adjective (a leisurely walk) and adverb; there is no leisurelily. The adverb sounds a little bookish, and at a leisurely pace is the everyday choice: We walked at a leisurely pace.

entries.meaning: In the direction of the longest side of something. ---
examples: Cut the zucchini in half lengthwise.
Fold the paper lengthwise, then open it again.
Lay the boards lengthwise across the truck bed.
entries.modifies: verbs such as cut, fold, lay

entries.meaning: In a way that is less strict or severe than expected. ---
examples: The judge treated him leniently because it was his first offense.
Teachers tend to grade leniently in the first semester.
The dress code is applied leniently to new employees.
entries.modifies: verbs such as treat, judge, grade, punish

entries.meaning: And certainly not — introducing something even less likely than what was just denied. ---
examples: I can't afford a car, let alone a house.
He can barely walk, let alone run a marathon.
Most people have never heard of the town, let alone visited it.
entries.русский: не говоря уже о, тем более
entries.type: linking — adds a stronger case after a negative
entries.position: end — after a negative clause, before the stronger case
entries.modifies: a noun, verb or phrase added to a negative statement
entries.contrast: Used only after a negative or near-negative: I can't boil an egg, let alone cook dinner. After a positive statement use not to mention. Don't confuse with leave someone alone (оставить в покое).

entries.meaning: Slowly and without energy or interest. ---
examples: He moved lethargically around the kitchen after the night shift.
The dog lay lethargically in the shade.
She shrugged lethargically and went back to her phone.

entries.meaning: In a crude, sexually offensive way. ---
examples: He winked lewdly at the waitress.
The comedian joked lewdly about his ex-wife.
Two men whistled lewdly as she walked past.

entries.meaning: Liberally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Apply sunscreen liberally before you go outside.
The chef uses garlic liberally in almost every dish.
The report is liberally sprinkled with charts and photos.
The court interpreted the law liberally.
The movie is liberally adapted from the novel.

senses.head: In large amounts; generously
examples: Apply sunscreen liberally before you go outside.
The chef uses garlic liberally in almost every dish.
The report is liberally sprinkled with charts and photos.

senses.head: Not strictly or literally; freely
examples: The court interpreted the law liberally.
The movie is liberally adapted from the novel.

entries.contrast: A false friend: Russian либерально suggests politics, but in everyday English liberally almost always means generously, in large amounts: Apply sunscreen liberally. The political idea is usually said with the adjective: She votes liberal, a liberal policy.

entries.meaning: As if dead; without movement, energy or feeling. ---
examples: His arm hung lifelessly over the side of the bed.
The flag drooped lifelessly in the still air.
She read the speech lifelessly, as if it were a grocery list.
entries.modifies: verbs such as hang, lie, speak

entries.meaning: With little luggage or weight; without carrying or eating much. ---
examples: I always travel light — just a backpack.
Pack light; the airline charges for every bag.
Next time I'm going to pack lighter.
entries.modifies: a few verbs: travel, pack, eat
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective light
entries.contrast: The flat adverb light lives in a few set phrases: travel light, pack light, eat light. Everywhere else use lightly: She touched his arm lightly, not touched his arm light. light in a light bag or a light color is the adjective.

entries.meaning: In a cheerful, joking way; without being serious. ---
examples: She light-heartedly teased him about his new haircut.
He talked light-heartedly about the accident, but he was clearly shaken.
The speech began light-heartedly before turning serious.
entries.form: -ly from lighthearted; American writing often closes it up as lightheartedly

entries.meaning: Lightly has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She knocked lightly on the door.
Lightly brush the dough with melted butter.
It was snowing lightly when we left the house.
Don't take his threats lightly.
This is not a decision we made lightly.
He got off lightly with just a warning.
Compared to the other houses on our street, we got off lightly in the storm.

senses.head: Gently, with little force or weight; a little
examples: She knocked lightly on the door.
Lightly brush the dough with melted butter.
It was snowing lightly when we left the house.

senses.head: Without being serious or thinking carefully
examples: Don't take his threats lightly.
This is not a decision we made lightly.

senses.head: With less punishment or harm than expected — in get off lightly
examples: He got off lightly with just a warning.
Compared to the other houses on our street, we got off lightly in the storm.

entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle (lightly salted)
entries.contrast: travel light / pack light keep the flat form, but touch lightly, knock lightly, lightly salted take -ly. take something lightly means not seriously (легкомысленно относиться), and not lightly means after serious thought: We didn't make this decision lightly.

entries.meaning: Smoothly, regularly and exactly as planned. ---
examples: The whole event went off like clockwork.
Every morning at six, like clockwork, the neighbor's dog starts barking.
Her paycheck arrives like clockwork on the first of the month.

entries.meaning: Very much, very fast or very hard. ---
examples: We had to work like crazy to finish on time.
It's been raining like crazy all week.
Tickets are selling like crazy.
entries.русский: как сумасшедший, бешено, изо всех сил
entries.type: degree — very much, very hard; informal

entries.meaning: Like hell has 2 distinct senses.
examples: When the dog started barking, we ran like hell.
My knee hurts like hell.
They fought like hell to keep the factory open.
“You're paying for this.” “Like hell I am!”
Like hell he was sick — I saw him at the game.

senses.head: Very hard, very fast or very much
examples: When the dog started barking, we ran like hell.
My knee hurts like hell.
They fought like hell to keep the factory open.

senses.head: Certainly not — a strong refusal or disbelief, at the front of a sentence
examples: “You're paying for this.” “Like hell I am!”
Like hell he was sick — I saw him at the game.

entries.русский: чертовски, изо всех сил; чёрта с два
entries.position: end — front in the refusal sense
entries.modifies: a verb; in the refusal sense, a whole clause
entries.contrast: Mildly vulgar; avoid it at work or in writing. Like crazy is the polite version of the first sense.

entries.meaning: Very fast, very hard, or very much. ---
examples: We ran like mad to catch the bus.
It's been snowing like mad since noon.
Everyone was working like mad before the deadline.
entries.contrast: Informal. Like crazy is the more common American equivalent and means the same. Neither suggests anger.

entries.meaning: Softly and without strength, firmness or energy. ---
examples: The flowers hung limply in the heat.
He shook my hand limply and looked away.
Her wet hair fell limply over her face.
entries.modifies: verbs such as hang, fall, shake hands

entries.meaning: At a steady, proportional rate, or in a straight step-by-step order. ---
examples: The cost grows linearly with the number of users.
The story isn't told linearly; it jumps back and forth in time.
Prices rose almost linearly over the decade.
entries.modifies: verbs such as grow, increase, tell

entries.meaning: In terms of language. ---
examples: Queens is linguistically diverse — well over a hundred languages are spoken there.
Linguistically, Romanian is closer to Italian than to its neighbors.
Children who are linguistically gifted often pick up a second language fast.
entries.position: front or end — before its word (linguistically diverse)

entries.meaning: Without energy or interest in anything. ---
examples: He flipped listlessly through the channels.
The kids sat listlessly in the heat, too tired to play.
She stirred her coffee listlessly and stared out the window.

entries.meaning: Gradually, in small amounts or steps. ---
examples: Little by little, the town was rebuilt.
She's getting her strength back little by little.
Save a bit each month, and little by little it adds up.
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause

entries.meaning: At the time something is actually happening, not recorded; in person. ---
examples: The game will be broadcast live on Channel 5.
I've never seen them play live.
We're going live now to our reporter in Chicago.
entries.modifies: verbs such as broadcast, perform, play, go
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective live (rhymes with five)
entries.contrast: The adverb and adjective live are pronounced /laɪv/, like five; the verb live (I live in Ohio) is /lɪv/, like give. watch it live = as it happens (в прямом эфире); see a band live = in person, not recorded (вживую).

entries.meaning: Locally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We buy most of our vegetables locally.
The restaurant only uses locally grown produce.
She's well known locally but not outside the county.
The cream should be applied locally to the rash.
Thunderstorms could be locally severe this afternoon.

senses.head: In or near the area where you are or that you are talking about
examples: We buy most of our vegetables locally.
The restaurant only uses locally grown produce.
She's well known locally but not outside the county.

senses.head: In one part or area only, not everywhere
examples: The cream should be applied locally to the rash.
Thunderstorms could be locally severe this afternoon.

entries.русский: на месте, в этом районе; местами
entries.position: end — before a past participle (locally grown)

entries.meaning: In a proud, superior way, or in grand, high-sounding terms. ---
examples: "I don't watch television," she said loftily.
He loftily dismissed his critics as amateurs.
The brochure speaks loftily of transforming lives but gives no details.

entries.meaning: Logically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Try to think logically about the problem.
He explained each step logically and slowly.
The essay isn't logically organized.
Logically, if he left at noon, he should be here by now.
Logically, the next step would be to raise prices.

senses.head: In a clear, reasoned way
examples: Try to think logically about the problem.
He explained each step logically and slowly.
The essay isn't logically organized.

senses.head: As follows from the facts; as you would reasonably expect
examples: Logically, if he left at noon, he should be here by now.
Logically, the next step would be to raise prices.

entries.position: end — front as a sentence adverb (Logically, …)

entries.meaning: A long time in the past. ---
examples: They moved away long ago.
Long ago, this whole valley was farmland.
I stopped worrying about that long ago.
entries.contrast: Like ago, it takes the simple past, never the present perfect: ✗ I have met him long ago. For something still true, use for a long time: I have lived here for a long time.

entries.meaning: Long ago, with the result still true now. ---
examples: The factory has long since closed.
The old debts were long since paid off.
Those friends have long since moved away.
entries.type: time — a long time ago, and still true now
entries.position: mid — usually with a perfect or passive verb (has long since closed)
entries.contrast: Since long is not English (a calque of с давних пор): say for a long time or long ago.

entries.meaning: Longer has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Can you stay a little longer?
The drive took longer than we expected.
Bake it ten minutes longer if you like it crispy.
He no longer works here.
I can't wait any longer.

senses.head: For a greater amount of time
examples: Can you stay a little longer?
The drive took longer than we expected.
Bake it ten minutes longer if you like it crispy.

senses.head: Not now, though it was true before — in no longer and not … any longer
examples: He no longer works here.
I can't wait any longer.

entries.type: duration; also time in no longer and any longer
entries.position: end — mid in no longer (She no longer works here)
entries.comparison: not gradable — it is already the comparative of long (much longer)
entries.form: comparative of long; the superlative is longest
entries.contrast: For time use longer, not more: Stay a little longer (останься подольше), not Stay more. Russian больше не / уже не is no longer before the verb (He no longer lives here) or not … any longer at the end (He doesn't live here any longer), never more not. no longer sounds a little more formal than not … anymore.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you want something very much. ---
examples: The kids stared longingly at the ice cream truck.
She talks longingly about the summers she spent in Maine.
He looked longingly at the last slice of pizza.
entries.modifies: verbs such as look, gaze, talk

entries.meaning: Loosely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Tie the rope loosely around the post.
Her hair hung loosely over her shoulders.
The movie is loosely based on a true story.
People use the word loosely to mean any kind of app.

senses.head: Not tightly or firmly
examples: Tie the rope loosely around the post.
Her hair hung loosely over her shoulders.

senses.head: Not exactly; in an approximate or free way
examples: The movie is loosely based on a true story.
People use the word loosely to mean any kind of app.

entries.position: mid or end — loosely based, tied loosely
