entries.form: most + importantly, the superlative of importantly
entries.contrast: Most important, … is also correct, and some editors prefer it. Use more importantly when adding a second, bigger point to one already made.

entries.meaning: In a very sad way, as if grieving. ---
examples: The dog howled mournfully at the door.
A train whistle sounded mournfully in the distance.
She looked mournfully at the empty chair.

entries.meaning: In a way that stirs strong feelings, especially sadness or sympathy. ---
examples: She spoke movingly about her late father.
The book describes the refugees' journey movingly.
He wrote movingly of his years in the war.

entries.meaning: With several countries or parties taking part together. ---
examples: The president said the problem must be solved multilaterally.
The sanctions were agreed multilaterally at the summit.
Trade rules work best when they are negotiated multilaterally.
entries.type: manner — involving several countries or groups

entries.meaning: In several ways or to several degrees at once. ---
examples: Paramedics took two multiply injured victims to the trauma center.
The school serves multiply disabled children from across the county.
Doctors are worried about multiply resistant strains of TB.
entries.type: degree — in more than one way
entries.position: before its word — a participle or adjective (multiply injured)
entries.form: from multiple, with -le becoming -ly, like doubly and triply
entries.contrast: Spelled exactly like the verb multiply (MUHL-tuh-ply, умножать), but the adverb ends in -plee. It is formal and appears almost only before a participle or adjective: multiply injured, multiply disabled, multiply resistant.

entries.meaning: By or under the control of a city or town government. ---
examples: The town gets power from a municipally owned utility.
Most of the parks are municipally run.
The golf course is municipally operated and open to everyone.
entries.type: manner — by a city or town government

entries.meaning: In a way that shows a wish to kill or hurt someone; savagely. ---
examples: She glared murderously at the driver who cut her off.
The two gangs fought murderously for control of the block.
He looked at me murderously when I told the story.

entries.meaning: In terms of music; as far as music is concerned. ---
examples: Musically, the new album is their best work.
Both of her kids are musically gifted.
The show looks great, but musically it's weak.
entries.position: front or end — front as a viewpoint (Musically, …); before its word in musically gifted

entries.meaning: In a thoughtful, slightly dreamy way, as if thinking aloud. ---
examples: "I wonder what ever happened to her," he said musingly.
She gazed musingly out at the lake.
He tapped his pen musingly against the desk.

entries.meaning: Without speaking. ---
examples: He nodded mutely and left the room.
The kids stared mutely at the broken window.
She shook her head mutely, too upset to answer.
entries.modifies: verbs, especially nod, stare, shake one's head

entries.meaning: In a way that is felt, done or shared by each side toward the other. ---
examples: The deal is mutually beneficial for both companies.
We set a mutually convenient time for the meeting.
The two plans are mutually exclusive — we can only choose one.
entries.type: manner — shared by both or all sides
entries.position: before its word — mutually beneficial, mutually agreed

entries.meaning: In a strange way that nobody can explain or understand. ---
examples: My keys mysteriously disappeared from the table.
She smiled mysteriously and changed the subject.
Mysteriously, the lights came back on by themselves.
entries.position: any position — end or mid for manner; front as a comment (Mysteriously, …)

entries.meaning: In a spiritual way that goes beyond ordinary understanding. ---
examples: Many visitors describe the canyon as mystically beautiful.
The poet writes mystically about nature and God.
The two lovers felt mystically connected.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows too little experience and too much trust. ---
examples: I naively believed the landlord would fix the heat.
She trusted him naively and lost her savings.
We naively assumed the drive would take two hours.

entries.meaning: Openly, without any attempt to hide it — usually about something unpleasant. ---
examples: The ad was a nakedly political attack.
He was nakedly ambitious from his first day on the job.
Her fear showed nakedly on her face.
entries.position: before its word — nakedly ambitious; also end

entries.meaning: Narrowly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The driver narrowly avoided hitting a deer.
The bill narrowly passed the Senate, 51 to 49.
She narrowly missed the bus.
The law defines "family" very narrowly.
Try not to think about the problem so narrowly.

senses.head: Only just; by a very small margin
examples: The driver narrowly avoided hitting a deer.
The bill narrowly passed the Senate, 51 to 49.
She narrowly missed the bus.

senses.head: In a strict or limited way
examples: The law defines "family" very narrowly.
Try not to think about the problem so narrowly.

entries.position: mid — before the verb (narrowly escaped); before its word in narrowly defined

entries.meaning: Nasally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He talks a little nasally when he has a cold.
The singer pronounced the vowels nasally.
The vaccine is given nasally instead of by shot.
This spray should be used nasally twice a day.

senses.head: With a sound that comes through the nose
examples: He talks a little nasally when he has a cold.
The singer pronounced the vowels nasally.

senses.head: Through the nose — about taking medicine
examples: The vaccine is given nasally instead of by shot.
This spray should be used nasally twice a day.

entries.comparison: more/most — in the speech sense only

entries.meaning: In a mean, unkind or unpleasant way. ---
examples: "Nobody asked you," she said nastily.
He laughed nastily at my mistake.
The argument ended nastily, with both of them yelling.

entries.meaning: Across or throughout a whole country; at the level of the country. ---
examples: The game will be nationally televised on Sunday.
Locally the store is popular, but nationally it's unknown.
The school is ranked 12th nationally.
entries.русский: по всей стране, на национальном уровне
entries.type: place — across a whole country; also viewpoint
entries.position: end; before its word in nationally televised

entries.meaning: In every part of a country. ---
examples: The movie opens nationwide on Friday.
The company has 300 stores nationwide.
Gas prices rose nationwide last month.
entries.contrast: The same form is an adjective before a noun: a nationwide search (общенациональный). As an adverb it follows the verb: The movie opens nationwide on Friday, not opens in nationwide.

entries.meaning: In a neat, stylish way — about clothes. ---
examples: A nattily dressed man held the door for us.
He showed up nattily attired in a bow tie.
The band was nattily dressed in matching suits.
entries.position: before its word — almost always nattily dressed

entries.meaning: In a badly behaved or slightly improper way — often playfully. ---
examples: The puppy naughtily chewed up my slippers.
She grinned naughtily and took the last cookie.
The kids in the back row giggled naughtily during the speech.

entries.meaning: Neatly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The towels were neatly folded on the bed.
Please write your name neatly at the top.
His clothes hung neatly in the closet.
That quote neatly sums up the whole book.
She neatly avoided answering the question.

senses.head: In a tidy, careful and orderly way
examples: The towels were neatly folded on the bed.
Please write your name neatly at the top.
His clothes hung neatly in the closet.

senses.head: Cleverly and exactly; in a simple, skillful way
examples: That quote neatly sums up the whole book.
She neatly avoided answering the question.

entries.meaning: Necessarily has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Expensive wine isn't necessarily better.
"So you're quitting?" "Not necessarily."
A quiet kid doesn't necessarily have a problem.
A bigger house necessarily means higher bills.
The summary is necessarily brief.

senses.head: In every case; for certain — almost always with not
body: (обязательно; not necessarily — не обязательно, не всегда)
examples: Expensive wine isn't necessarily better.
"So you're quitting?" "Not necessarily."
A quiet kid doesn't necessarily have a problem.

senses.head: As a result that cannot be avoided
examples: A bigger house necessarily means higher bills.
The summary is necessarily brief.

entries.русский: обязательно, непременно (чаще not necessarily — не обязательно)
entries.position: mid — after not or the first auxiliary (doesn't necessarily mean)
entries.contrast: Most often negative: not necessarily = не обязательно, не всегда. Do not use it for Russian обязательно in a request or promise: Обязательно приходи! is Be sure to come! or You have to come!, not Necessarily come!; Я обязательно позвоню is I'll definitely call. On its own, necessarily means “as a logical result”, which is formal.

entries.meaning: Exactly even in a race or competition. ---
examples: The two candidates are running neck and neck in the polls.
The horses came down the stretch neck and neck.
Sales of the two phones have been neck and neck all year.
entries.русский: ноздря в ноздрю, голова в голову
entries.type: manner — exactly even in a race or contest
entries.modifies: verbs such as run, be, finish

entries.meaning: Without any good reason; more than is necessary. ---
examples: The form is needlessly complicated.
Hundreds of people died needlessly in the fire.
Don't worry him needlessly — wait until we know more.
entries.position: mid; before its word in needlessly complicated

entries.meaning: Negatively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Lack of sleep can negatively affect your memory.
Voters reacted negatively to the tax plan.
Try not to think so negatively about yourself.
Electrons are negatively charged.
The negatively charged ions move toward the positive pole.

senses.head: In a bad, harmful or disapproving way
examples: Lack of sleep can negatively affect your memory.
Voters reacted negatively to the tax plan.
Try not to think so negatively about yourself.

senses.head: With a negative electric charge
examples: Electrons are negatively charged.
The negatively charged ions move toward the positive pole.

entries.position: end; mid before affect and impact

entries.meaning: Without the proper care that is expected, often with legal responsibility. ---
examples: The lawsuit claims the hospital acted negligently.
He was accused of driving negligently through a school zone.
The landlord negligently ignored the broken railing.

entries.meaning: In a worried, anxious or uneasy way. ---
examples: She laughed nervously and looked at the floor.
He waited nervously outside the principal's office.
The kids glanced nervously at the dark woods.

entries.meaning: In an overly anxious or obsessive way. ---
examples: He neurotically checks the stove five times before leaving.
She is neurotically afraid of germs.
I planned every minute of the trip neurotically.

entries.meaning: Not at any time in the future. ---
examples: Never again will I fly that airline.
I'll never again lend him money.
She promised herself she would never again work weekends.
entries.position: any position — front with inversion, or mid
entries.contrast: Fronted, it forces inversion like never: Never again will I…, not ✗ Never again I will…. In mid position the order is normal: I will never again….

entries.meaning: Recently; not long ago. ---
examples: The newly elected mayor gave her first speech.
They're newly married and still looking for a house.
We ate at a newly opened Thai place downtown.
entries.position: before its word — a past participle (newly built, newly elected)
entries.contrast: newly goes only before a participle or adjective: newly married, a newly opened store. It does not modify a finite verb — He just arrived or He arrived recently, not He newly arrived.

entries.meaning: In or into the house, apartment or room beside this one. ---
examples: A young couple just moved in next door.
The kids next door are always playing basketball.
I ran next door to borrow some sugar.
entries.type: place — in the next house, apartment or room
entries.modifies: a verb, or a noun it follows (the kids next door)
entries.contrast: Next door is the adverb; next-door with a hyphen is the adjective (our next-door neighbors); next door to works as a preposition (She lives next door to us).

entries.meaning: Nicely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Your garden is coming along nicely.
The dress fits you nicely.
The rice turned out nicely.
If you ask nicely, I'll give you a cookie.
Please treat your little brother nicely.

senses.head: Well; in a pleasant or satisfactory way
examples: Your garden is coming along nicely.
The dress fits you nicely.
The rice turned out nicely.

senses.head: Politely or kindly
examples: If you ask nicely, I'll give you a cookie.
Please treat your little brother nicely.

entries.meaning: Quickly, lightly and easily in movement or thought. ---
examples: The goat climbed nimbly up the rocks.
Her fingers moved nimbly over the keys.
The senator nimbly dodged the reporter's question.

entries.meaning: By nine times as much. ---
examples: Online orders jumped ninefold in a single year.
The town's population has grown almost ninefold since 1950.
The cost of the project increased ninefold from the first estimate.
entries.modifies: verbs such as increase, grow, rise

entries.meaning: Probably; I am fairly sure. ---
examples: No doubt you've already heard the news.
He'll be late again, no doubt.
The team will no doubt be disappointed.
entries.type: stance — the speaker thinks something is very likely
entries.contrast: Weaker than it looks: No doubt you've heard the news means I suppose you have (наверняка). For real certainty say without a doubt or undoubtedly.

entries.meaning: Not now, though it was true before. ---
examples: She no longer works here.
The store is no longer open on Sundays.
I can no longer remember his name.
entries.type: time — something that was true has stopped
entries.contrast: No longer goes in mid position with a positive verb (She no longer works here); not … anymore goes at the end (She doesn't work here anymore). Never both: She doesn't no longer work here is wrong. Russian больше не tempts learners toward no more, which sounds literary here.

entries.meaning: In a brave, generous or honorable way. ---
examples: The firefighters acted nobly during the crisis.
He nobly offered to take the blame.
She fought nobly for the rights of workers.

entries.meaning: At night rather than during the day — mostly about animals. ---
examples: Most owls hunt nocturnally.
In the desert, many animals are active nocturnally to avoid the heat.
Raccoons feed nocturnally and sleep through the day.
entries.modifies: verbs such as hunt, feed, be active

entries.meaning: Without making any sound. ---
examples: The cat moved noiselessly across the rug.
The electric car pulled away noiselessly.
He closed the door noiselessly behind him.

entries.meaning: With a lot of noise; loudly. ---
examples: The kids ran noisily down the hall.
He slurped his soup noisily.
The old refrigerator hums noisily all night.

entries.meaning: In name or on paper, but not in reality. ---
examples: The king is nominally the head of state.
She was nominally in charge, but her deputy made the decisions.
The country is nominally a democracy.
entries.position: before its word — nominally in charge; also mid

entries.meaning: Calmly and casually, as if not worried or interested. ---
examples: He leaned nonchalantly against the wall.
"Oh, I won the lottery," she said nonchalantly.
The cat walked nonchalantly past the barking dog.

entries.meaning: Nonstop has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The baby cried nonstop for two hours.
It rained nonstop all weekend.
She talks nonstop about her new job.
We flew nonstop from Chicago to Rome.
This bus goes nonstop to the airport.

senses.head: Without stopping or pausing
examples: The baby cried nonstop for two hours.
It rained nonstop all weekend.
She talks nonstop about her new job.

senses.head: Without stopping on the way — about a trip
examples: We flew nonstop from Chicago to Rome.
This bus goes nonstop to the airport.

entries.contrast: The same form is an adjective: a nonstop flight (прямой рейс). As an adverb: We flew nonstop to Tokyo.

entries.meaning: Without words — through gestures, facial expressions or body language. ---
examples: Babies communicate nonverbally long before they talk.
He showed his anger nonverbally, by crossing his arms.
Much of what we say, we say nonverbally.

entries.meaning: Without using force or violence. ---
examples: The marchers protested nonviolently in front of city hall.
Dr. King urged people to resist nonviolently.
The standoff ended nonviolently.

entries.meaning: Toward or in the north. ---
examples: We drove north along the coast.
Birds fly north in the spring.
The town lies about fifty miles north of Denver.
entries.modifies: verbs of motion, and be, live, lie
entries.contrast: As an adverb it takes no preposition: drive north, head north, not drive to north. Use to the north or in the north when it is a noun: They live in the north of the state. up north is common in American speech: We have a cabin up north.

entries.meaning: Toward or in the northeast. ---
examples: The storm is moving northeast.
The farm is ten miles northeast of town.
Head northeast until you reach the lake.
entries.modifies: verbs of motion, and be, live, lie
entries.form: north + east, written as one word in American English

entries.meaning: Toward or in the northwest. ---
examples: The trail turns northwest after the bridge.
They moved northwest, to Seattle.
The airport is about twenty miles northwest of the city.
entries.modifies: verbs of motion, and be, live, lie
entries.form: north + west, written as one word in American English

entries.meaning: With a fond, slightly sad longing for the past. ---
examples: My grandfather talks nostalgically about his childhood farm.
She looked back nostalgically on her college years.
The movie nostalgically recreates small-town life in the 1950s.
entries.modifies: verbs, especially talk, remember, look back

entries.meaning: And also — adding something that makes the point stronger. ---
examples: The house needs a new roof, not to mention new windows.
She speaks French and Spanish, not to mention a little Japanese.
Driving downtown costs a fortune in gas, not to mention parking.
entries.position: end — before the item it adds
entries.modifies: a noun, adjective or phrase added to the statement
entries.contrast: Unlike let alone, it works after positive statements: The hotel was expensive, not to mention noisy.

entries.meaning: Not at all; in no way — in nothing like. ---
examples: She looks nothing like her sister.
The hotel was nothing like the pictures online.
Honestly, it tastes nothing like real chicken.
entries.type: negative — in no way, not at all
entries.position: before its word — almost only nothing like
entries.modifies: like and close to phrases after be, look, sound, taste
entries.contrast: Usually nothing is a pronoun: I saw nothing. The adverb use is fixed: She looks nothing like her sister = совсем не похожа. It already carries the negative, so no not: It's nothing like the photo or It isn't anything like the photo, never It isn't nothing like.

entries.meaning: In a way that is easy to see or notice. ---
examples: It's noticeably cooler in the mountains.
Her English has improved noticeably this year.
He was noticeably absent from the party.
entries.position: before its word — noticeably better; also mid

entries.meaning: In a way that is widely known — about something bad or difficult. ---
examples: Parking downtown is notoriously difficult.
The weather in Chicago is notoriously unpredictable.
That airline is notoriously late.
entries.position: before its word — notoriously difficult; also mid
entries.contrast: notoriously is always negative: notoriously unreliable = печально известен своей ненадёжностью. For something good use famously or well known for: famously generous, not notoriously generous.

entries.meaning: Nevertheless; in spite of that. ---
examples: The reviews were terrible; the movie made millions notwithstanding.
The plan has real risks. Notwithstanding, the board voted to go ahead.
Many people objected, but the council approved the project notwithstanding.
entries.русский: тем не менее, несмотря на это
entries.type: linking — contrast: in spite of what was just said
entries.contrast: Usually a preposition, before or after its noun: notwithstanding the cost, the cost notwithstanding (несмотря на). Only when it stands alone, with nothing after it, is it the adverb meaning nevertheless. Both uses are formal; in speech Americans say still, even so or despite that.

entries.meaning: Sometimes, but not regularly or often. ---
examples: We still have lunch together now and again.
Now and again, a car drove past the house.
It's fine to skip the gym now and again.
entries.position: end — or front, often as every now and again
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause

entries.meaning: Sometimes, but not often. ---
examples: I still see him now and then.
Every now and then, she calls to check on me.
It's nice to eat out now and then.
entries.position: end — or front, often as every now and then
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause
entries.contrast: Now and again, every now and then and every so often mean the same.

entries.meaning: Without feeling or reacting, as if in shock. ---
examples: She stared numbly at the letter.
He nodded numbly as the doctor explained.
We walked numbly out of the hospital.
entries.form: -ly from numb; the b is silent

entries.meaning: In terms of numbers; by number. ---
examples: The files are sorted numerically, not by date.
The enemy was numerically stronger but poorly trained.
Express the results numerically in a table.
entries.position: end; before its word in numerically superior

entries.meaning: In terms of the nutrients food contains. ---
examples: School lunches must be nutritionally balanced.
Nutritionally, brown rice beats white rice.
Canned beans are nutritionally similar to dried ones.
entries.русский: с точки зрения питания, по питательности
entries.position: before its word — nutritionally balanced; also front

entries.meaning: Used after a number from one to twelve to name an exact hour. ---
examples: The store opens at nine o'clock.
It's almost three o'clock — we're going to be late.
I'll meet you at the station at six o'clock.
entries.position: after its word — after a number from one to twelve
entries.contrast: Only with whole hours: at six o'clock, but at 6:30 or at half past six, never 6:30 o'clock. Do not add a.m. or p.m.: say 7 p.m. or seven o'clock in the evening, not 7 o'clock p.m. Russian в шесть часов is at six o'clock or just at six.

entries.meaning: In a way that does what you are told. ---
examples: The dog sat obediently by the door.
The students obediently lined up in the hall.
She obediently handed over her phone.

entries.meaning: Fairly, based on facts and not on personal feelings. ---
examples: Try to look at the situation objectively.
Objectively, it was the better offer.
Judges are supposed to decide cases objectively.
entries.position: any position — end for manner; front as a comment (Objectively, …)

entries.meaning: In a willing, helpful way. ---
examples: The waiter obligingly moved us to a quieter table.
A stranger obligingly took our picture.
The dog rolled over obligingly when the kids asked.

entries.meaning: Obliquely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The speech referred only obliquely to the scandal.
She hinted obliquely that she might leave the company.
Late afternoon light fell obliquely across the floor.
The road crosses the river obliquely.

senses.head: Indirectly, without saying something openly
examples: The speech referred only obliquely to the scandal.
She hinted obliquely that she might leave the company.

senses.head: At an angle; not straight
examples: Late afternoon light fell obliquely across the floor.
The road crosses the river obliquely.

entries.meaning: In a very annoying or rude way. ---
examples: The guy behind us talked obnoxiously through the whole movie.
Their music was obnoxiously loud.
He bragged obnoxiously about his new car.
entries.position: end; before its word in obnoxiously loud

entries.meaning: Obscenely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Some CEOs are paid obscenely high salaries.
The family is obscenely rich.
Tickets were obscenely expensive.
A fan gestured obscenely at the referee.
He was fined for swearing obscenely on live TV.

senses.head: Shockingly, unfairly much — about money or excess
examples: Some CEOs are paid obscenely high salaries.
The family is obscenely rich.
Tickets were obscenely expensive.

senses.head: In a sexually offensive or indecent way
examples: A fan gestured obscenely at the referee.
He was fined for swearing obscenely on live TV.

entries.position: before its word — obscenely rich; end in the manner sense
entries.modifies: adjectives; verbs in the manner sense

entries.meaning: Obscurely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The rule is so obscurely worded that nobody follows it.
He hinted obscurely at trouble in the family.
She felt obscurely guilty, though she had done nothing wrong.
I was obscurely disappointed by the ending.

senses.head: In a way that is unclear or hard to understand
examples: The rule is so obscurely worded that nobody follows it.
He hinted obscurely at trouble in the family.

senses.head: In a vague way that you cannot quite explain — about feelings
examples: She felt obscurely guilty, though she had done nothing wrong.
I was obscurely disappointed by the ending.

entries.position: end; before its word in obscurely worded

entries.meaning: Too eager to please or obey, in a way that seems insincere. ---
examples: The manager smiled obsequiously at the rich customer.
He agreed obsequiously with everything his boss said.
The staff bowed obsequiously as the senator walked in.

entries.meaning: In a way that cannot stop thinking about or doing something. ---
examples: She checks her email obsessively.
He is obsessively neat about his desk.
Fans followed the trial obsessively.

entries.meaning: Stubbornly, refusing to change your mind. ---
examples: He obstinately refused to see a doctor.
The toddler shook her head obstinately.
Prices have stayed obstinately high.

entries.meaning: Oddly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's been acting oddly since the accident.
The house was oddly quiet when we got home.
She was dressed oddly for a job interview.
Oddly enough, I wasn't nervous at all.
Oddly, nobody noticed the missing painting for a week.

senses.head: In a strange or unusual way
examples: He's been acting oddly since the accident.
The house was oddly quiet when we got home.
She was dressed oddly for a job interview.

senses.head: Surprisingly — commenting on a whole statement, often oddly enough
examples: Oddly enough, I wasn't nervous at all.
Oddly, nobody noticed the missing painting for a week.

entries.position: any position — end for manner; front as a comment (Oddly enough, …)

entries.meaning: Ever; in the whole of history — after a superlative. ---
examples: Many fans call him the greatest basketball player of all time.
It became the best-selling album of all time.
What's your favorite movie of all time?
entries.type: time — ever, in the whole of history
entries.position: after its word — right after a superlative noun phrase
entries.modifies: a noun phrase with a superlative (the best … of all time)
entries.contrast: Russian всех времён is often rendered of all times; the English phrase is singular: the greatest player of all time. Of all time follows the noun; ever can follow it too (the best movie ever).

entries.meaning: Certainly; as expected or as anyone would know. ---
examples: Of course you can bring a friend.
“Can you help me move on Saturday?” “Of course.”
He was late, of course, and blamed the traffic.
entries.type: stance — the speaker treats something as expected or obvious
entries.modifies: a whole clause, or stands alone as a reply
entries.contrast: As a reply to a request it is warm (Can I borrow a pen? — Of course). As a reply to a question of fact it can sound like obviously, you should know that: Is this your first time here? — Of course! can come across as rude. Russian конечно is softer; for a neutral yes say Sure or Yes, it is.

entries.meaning: Recently; in the last few weeks or months. ---
examples: Her health has been poor of late.
Of late, the company has been cutting costs.
He's been rather quiet of late.
entries.modifies: a verb, usually in the present perfect
entries.contrast: Formal; in speech Americans say lately or recently.

entries.meaning: Occasionally, with breaks in between. ---
examples: It rained off and on all day.
They've dated off and on for years.
I've been working on the book off and on since 2019.
entries.contrast: On and off means exactly the same. Both describe an activity that keeps stopping and starting, not one that happens rarely — for that, use occasionally.

entries.meaning: Without preparing or thinking about it in advance. ---
examples: She spoke off the cuff for twenty minutes.
I'm just saying this off the cuff, so don't quote me.
The mayor answered the question off the cuff.
entries.contrast: Hyphenated before a noun: an off-the-cuff remark.

entries.meaning: Unofficially; not to be published or quoted. ---
examples: Off the record, the deal is already done.
The official spoke to reporters off the record.
Can I tell you something off the record?
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking, or a whole clause
entries.contrast: The opposite is on the record (официально, под запись). Hyphenated before a noun: off-the-record comments.

entries.meaning: Offensively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The comedian was accused of joking offensively about immigrants.
He behaved offensively toward the waitress.
Offensively, the team struggled all season.
They played well offensively but gave up too many goals.

senses.head: In a rude or insulting way
examples: The comedian was accused of joking offensively about immigrants.
He behaved offensively toward the waitress.

senses.head: In attack — especially in sports, about scoring points
examples: Offensively, the team struggled all season.
They played well offensively but gave up too many goals.

entries.position: end; front as a viewpoint in sports (Offensively, …)

entries.meaning: Without checking the facts or thinking about it first. ---
examples: I don't know his phone number offhand.
Offhand, I'd say it will cost about $500.
Can you remember offhand when the meeting starts?
entries.form: off + hand, written as one word
entries.contrast: Before a noun it is an adjective meaning careless or casual: an offhand remark (небрежное замечание). As an adverb it usually means from memory, right now: I don't know offhand.

entries.meaning: Casually, as if it were not important. ---
examples: She mentioned offhandedly that she was moving to Texas.
He offhandedly dismissed my idea.
"Oh, I got the job," he said offhandedly.

entries.meaning: In a bossy, self-important way, giving orders or help nobody asked for. ---
examples: A security guard officiously demanded to see our tickets again.
He officiously told everyone at the picnic where to park.
The clerk officiously pointed out a tiny mistake on my form.
entries.contrast: A false friend: officiously is not официально. That is officially. officiously is always critical — bossy and too eager to use a little authority.

entries.meaning: Offline has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You can read the articles offline on the plane.
The app still works offline.
The server went offline just before noon.
Let's discuss that offline.
We took the budget question offline after the call.

senses.head: Without a connection to the internet
examples: You can read the articles offline on the plane.
The app still works offline.
The server went offline just before noon.

senses.head: Privately, outside the current meeting or call
examples: Let's discuss that offline.
We took the budget question offline after the call.

entries.русский: офлайн, без подключения к интернету; отдельно, в частном порядке
entries.type: place — not on the internet; also manner
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective offline
entries.contrast: Sense 2 is office jargon: take it offline means talk about it later, just the people involved, and has nothing to do with the internet.

entries.meaning: Offstage has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The actor bowed and walked offstage.
We heard a crash offstage.
Offstage, the rock star is quiet and shy.
The two comedians were close friends offstage.

senses.head: Off the stage, where the audience cannot see
examples: The actor bowed and walked offstage.
We heard a crash offstage.

senses.head: In a performer's private life
examples: Offstage, the rock star is quiet and shy.
The two comedians were close friends offstage.

entries.русский: за кулисами, со сцены; в жизни
entries.position: end; front for the private-life sense (Offstage, …)
entries.form: off + stage, written as one word

entries.meaning: Often; many times. ---
examples: Oftentimes the simplest answer is the right one.
Kids oftentimes understand more than we think.
We'd oftentimes stay up talking until two in the morning.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb; also front (Oftentimes, …)
entries.contrast: An American word, common in speech and informal writing; British English treats it as old-fashioned. It means the same as often but cannot be compared or modified: more often, very often, never more oftentimes. In formal writing use often.

entries.meaning: Well enough; in an acceptable way. ---
examples: The interview went okay, I guess.
Is the printer working okay now?
She's doing okay after the surgery.
entries.contrast: As an adverb okay means acceptably, not especially well: The interview went okay = нормально, так себе, not отлично. It is informal; in careful writing use well or fine. Its uses as an adjective (Are you okay?) and an interjection (Okay, let's go) belong to other word classes.

entries.meaning: In a way that suggests something bad is going to happen. ---
examples: Dark clouds gathered ominously over the lake.
The engine made an ominously loud clunk.
The street was ominously quiet.
entries.position: end; mid before an adjective (ominously quiet)

entries.meaning: On the hands and knees. ---
examples: The baby crawled across the rug on all fours.
I was on all fours looking for my contact lens.
He got down on all fours so his daughter could ride on his back.

entries.meaning: At some times but not others, with breaks in between. ---
examples: It rained on and off all day.
They've been dating on and off for three years.
I worked there on and off during college.
entries.contrast: Off and on means the same. Before a noun: an on-and-off relationship, also on-again, off-again.

entries.meaning: Usually, or as a typical amount when many cases are considered. ---
examples: On average, the trip takes about forty minutes.
Women live longer than men on average.
We get about three inches of rain a month on average.
entries.type: viewpoint — as a typical or mean figure
entries.modifies: a whole clause, often one with a number
entries.contrast: On the average is the same, slightly older. Not in average, a common calque of в среднем.

entries.meaning: On board has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Once we were on board, the ferry left right away.
The captain made sure everyone was on board.
The flight attendants welcomed us on board.
Is your boss on board with the idea?
We need the whole department on board before we announce it.
We're happy to have her on board as our new CFO.

senses.head: On or in a ship, plane, train or bus
examples: Once we were on board, the ferry left right away.
The captain made sure everyone was on board.
The flight attendants welcomed us on board.

senses.head: Part of a team, or in agreement with a plan
examples: Is your boss on board with the idea?
We need the whole department on board before we announce it.
We're happy to have her on board as our new CFO.

entries.modifies: verbs such as be, get, come, have
entries.contrast: Followed by a noun it works as a preposition (on board the ship). Aboard means the same in the first sense.

entries.meaning: Used after a question word or a negative to add surprise, annoyance or emphasis. ---
examples: What on earth are you doing?
Why on earth would anyone buy that?
There's no reason on earth to worry.
entries.type: degree — an intensifier in questions and negatives
entries.position: after its word — right after what, why, where, who, how, or a negative noun phrase (no reason on earth)
entries.modifies: a question word or a negative noun phrase
entries.contrast: Shows surprise or annoyance: What on earth…? ≈ Что же…? / Какого чёрта…? In the world works the same way. In the happiest man on earth it is a literal phrase, not this adverb.

entries.meaning: Without asking for proof; by trusting. ---
examples: I can't just take your word on faith; show me the numbers.
Most of us accept what doctors tell us on faith.
The investors took the founder's promises on faith.
entries.position: end — usually in take or accept something on faith
entries.modifies: verbs such as take and accept

entries.meaning: Sometimes, but not often. ---
examples: I still eat meat on occasion.
On occasion, the manager works the register herself.
He can be rude on occasion.
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause

entries.meaning: According to documents or theory, though perhaps not in reality. ---
examples: On paper, it looked like the perfect plan.
He's a great candidate on paper, but the interview went badly.
The company is worth millions on paper.
entries.type: viewpoint — in theory or according to documents
entries.contrast: Also literal: put your thoughts on paper (записать).

entries.meaning: Intentionally; not by accident. ---
examples: He broke the vase on purpose!
Sorry, I didn't do it on purpose.
Did you leave the door open on purpose?
entries.contrast: Not by purpose. Russian специально has two meanings: on purpose (intentionally: He broke it on purpose) and specially, for one reason (I came just to see you).

entries.meaning: Not at all — the opposite is true. ---
examples: “You must be bored.” “On the contrary, I'm having a great time.”
The medicine didn't help; on the contrary, it made him worse.
I don't dislike her. On the contrary, I think she's great.
entries.type: linking — rejecting what was said and stating the opposite
entries.contrast: On the contrary rejects what was just said: You're not bothering me — on the contrary, I'm glad you came (наоборот). To compare two sides of one situation use on the other hand (с другой стороны). Mixing the two is a common learner error. To the contrary follows a noun: despite rumors to the contrary.

entries.meaning: At exactly the stated time. ---
examples: The meeting starts at nine on the dot.
She showed up at noon on the dot.
The train left at 6:15 on the dot.
entries.type: time — exactly at the stated time
entries.position: after its word — right after the clock time

entries.meaning: Judging by how something looks at first, which may not be the whole truth. ---
examples: On the face of it, the offer looks generous.
On the face of it, the two cases have nothing in common.
It seems, on the face of it, like a simple mistake.
entries.русский: на первый взгляд, судя по всему
entries.type: viewpoint — judging by how things appear

entries.meaning: Quickly, while something is already in progress, without planning ahead. ---
examples: We didn't have a plan, so we made decisions on the fly.
The app translates speech on the fly.
Good teachers adjust the lesson on the fly.
entries.type: manner — while something is already happening

entries.meaning: Exactly; precisely. ---
examples: She guessed the final score on the nose.
The bill came to fifty dollars on the nose.
We arrived at eight on the nose.
entries.position: after its word — right after a time or amount, or at the end
entries.modifies: a time, an amount, or a verb
entries.contrast: As an adjective phrase it also means too obvious, not subtle: The movie's message was a little on the nose.

entries.meaning: Introducing the first of two different or opposing points. ---
examples: On the one hand, the job pays well; on the other hand, the hours are long.
On the one hand, I'd love to travel. On the other, I hate flying.
I'm torn: on the one hand, I trust him; on the other, the facts don't add up.
entries.type: linking — introducing the first of two contrasting points
entries.contrast: Normally followed by on the other hand; on one hand without the is also common in American English.

entries.meaning: Introducing a different or opposite side of the same situation. ---
examples: The city is exciting. On the other hand, it's very expensive.
My brother loves sports; I, on the other hand, would rather read.
It's a great car. On the other hand, we can't really afford it.
entries.contrast: It adds another side of the same situation, not a correction; to reject what was said use on the contrary (наоборот). It is often used alone, without on the one hand.

entries.meaning: On the side has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He does repair work on the side.
She's a nurse but sells jewelry on the side.
He'd been seeing someone on the side for months.
Could I get the dressing on the side?
The steak comes with fries on the side.

senses.head: In addition to one's main job or relationship, often secretly
examples: He does repair work on the side.
She's a nurse but sells jewelry on the side.
He'd been seeing someone on the side for months.

senses.head: Served separately, not on top of the main food
examples: Could I get the dressing on the side?
The steak comes with fries on the side.

entries.modifies: a verb, or a noun it follows (fries on the side)

entries.meaning: Secretly, so that others don't notice. ---
examples: He's been smoking on the sly.
She read her sister's diary on the sly.
They were meeting on the sly after work.

entries.meaning: On the spot has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He was fired on the spot.
They offered me the job on the spot.
The officer wrote him a ticket on the spot.
The reporter's question really put the senator on the spot.
Sorry to put you on the spot, but could you say a few words?
Paramedics were on the spot within minutes.
Our reporter on the spot has the latest.

senses.head: Immediately, right then and there
examples: He was fired on the spot.
They offered me the job on the spot.
The officer wrote him a ticket on the spot.

senses.head: In a difficult position where one must answer or act at once — usually put someone on the spot
examples: The reporter's question really put the senator on the spot.
Sorry to put you on the spot, but could you say a few words?

senses.head: At the place where something is happening
examples: Paramedics were on the spot within minutes.
Our reporter on the spot has the latest.

entries.русский: сразу, на месте; в затруднительное положение
entries.modifies: a verb, or a noun it follows (a reporter on the spot)
entries.contrast: British run on the spot is run in place in American English.

entries.term: on the spur of the moment
entries.respell: ahn thuh SPUR uhv thuh MOH-muhnt
entries.meaning: Suddenly, without planning ahead. ---
examples: We decided to drive to the coast on the spur of the moment.
I bought the jacket on the spur of the moment and regretted it later.
On the spur of the moment, he asked her to marry him.

entries.meaning: On the way has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Let's grab coffee on the way to work.
I called my mom on the way home.
We got lost twice on the way.
Stay calm, help is on the way.
They have two kids and a third on the way.

senses.head: While traveling somewhere; during the trip
examples: Let's grab coffee on the way to work.
I called my mom on the way home.
We got lost twice on the way.

senses.head: Coming soon; about to arrive or happen
examples: Stay calm, help is on the way.
They have two kids and a third on the way.

entries.русский: по дороге, по пути; на подходе
entries.modifies: verbs of stopping and moving; be in help is on the way
entries.contrast: On the way means during a trip; in the way means blocking someone (Your bike is in the way); by the way introduces a side remark. Russian по дороге is on the way, never by the way.

entries.meaning: Generally; taking everything into account. ---
examples: On the whole, the trip went well.
The reviews were, on the whole, positive.
People here are friendly on the whole.
entries.type: viewpoint — a general judgment that allows exceptions
entries.position: front — also mid between commas or end
entries.contrast: On the whole sums up a judgment (в целом); as a whole follows a noun and means taken together: the country as a whole.

entries.meaning: At the scheduled time; not late. ---
examples: The flight left on time.
Please pay your rent on time.
She's never on time for meetings.
entries.modifies: verbs of arriving, leaving, paying, finishing
entries.contrast: On time means at the scheduled time, not late; in time means early enough, before it is too late: The train left on time, but We got there in time to say goodbye. Russian вовремя covers both.

entries.meaning: One more time; as has happened before. ---
examples: Once again, the bus was late.
Thank you once again for your help.
He has once again forgotten my birthday.
entries.type: frequency — one more time, often as before
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause

entries.meaning: Finally and completely, so it never has to be done again. ---
examples: Let's settle this once and for all.
I want to quit smoking once and for all.
The court ruling ended the dispute once and for all.
entries.position: end — sometimes before the verb it follows

entries.meaning: Sometimes, but not often. ---
examples: We eat out once in a while.
Once in a while I still think about her.
It's good to take a day off every once in a while.
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause
entries.form: also every once in a while

entries.meaning: One more time; again. ---
examples: Could you say that once more, slowly?
Let's go through the plan once more.
Once more, the team came back from behind.
entries.modifies: a verb or a whole clause

entries.meaning: In a series, each following the one before. ---
examples: The guests left one after another.
Problems kept coming up one after another.
She ate three cookies one after the other.

entries.meaning: Singly, each separately after the last. ---
examples: Please come in one at a time.
Take the pills one at a time, with water.
Let's deal with these problems one at a time.

entries.meaning: Separately and in turn, one following another. ---
examples: One by one, the lights in the building went out.
The teacher called the students up one by one.
We checked the boxes one by one.

entries.meaning: Between two people only, face to face. ---
examples: The coach meets one-on-one with every player.
I'd like to talk to you one-on-one after class.
The tutor works one-on-one with struggling readers.
entries.contrast: The same form is an adjective: a one-on-one meeting. British English says one-to-one; Americans say one-on-one.

entries.meaning: On or through the internet. ---
examples: I bought the tickets online.
She works online from her kitchen table.
More people shop online now than in stores.
entries.type: place — on the internet; also manner
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective online
entries.contrast: No preposition before it: buy online, meet online, never ✗ in online or ✗ in the online. Go online means connect to the internet. Written as one word; the older on-line is now rare.

entries.meaning: Very, completely; sometimes with regret that it is so. ---
examples: I'd be only too happy to help.
She knew only too well what would happen.
The danger is only too real.
entries.type: degree — very, often with a note of regret
entries.position: before its word — an adjective or well
entries.modifies: adjectives like happy, glad, aware, true; well
entries.contrast: Not only plus too: I'd be only too happy to help means very happy, not excessively happy. With well, aware or true it adds regret: I know that only too well (увы, слишком хорошо).

entries.meaning: Toward the land from the sea, or on land rather than at sea. ---
examples: The hurricane is expected to move onshore tonight.
The wind was blowing onshore, bringing in big waves.
Most of the company's oil is now produced onshore.
entries.form: on + shore, written as one word
entries.contrast: The opposite of offshore. The same form is an adjective: an onshore wind, onshore drilling.

entries.meaning: On or onto the stage, in front of the audience. ---
examples: The crowd cheered as the band walked onstage.
She's shy in person but fearless onstage.
He fell onstage during the second act.
entries.form: on + stage, written as one word

entries.meaning: Without hiding anything; publicly and honestly. ---
examples: We talked openly about our money problems.
He was the first openly gay member of the city council.
Several players openly criticized the coach.

entries.meaning: In terms of how an organization, system or machine works day to day. ---
examples: Operationally, the merger went smoothly.
The new plant will be operationally ready by June.
The airline is struggling operationally and financially.
entries.русский: в оперативном отношении, с точки зрения работы
entries.type: viewpoint — in terms of how something runs
entries.position: front or end; before its word in operationally ready

entries.meaning: Facing someone or something, on the other side. ---
examples: I took a seat, and my boss sat down opposite.
The man sitting opposite kept reading over my shoulder.
There's a school on the corner and a church directly opposite.
entries.modifies: verbs such as sit, live, stand
entries.contrast: Most often a preposition (the bank opposite the park) or an adjective (the opposite side). It is an adverb only when nothing follows: She sat down opposite. For buildings Americans more often say across the street: They live across the street sounds more natural than They live opposite.

entries.meaning: Oppressively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was oppressively hot and humid in New Orleans.
The room fell oppressively silent.
The regime ruled oppressively for forty years.
Workers said the company was managed oppressively.

senses.head: Unpleasantly and heavily — about heat, silence or an atmosphere
examples: It was oppressively hot and humid in New Orleans.
The room fell oppressively silent.

senses.head: Cruelly and unfairly, using power to control people
examples: The regime ruled oppressively for forty years.
Workers said the company was managed oppressively.

entries.position: before its word — oppressively hot; end in the manner sense
entries.modifies: adjectives; verbs in the manner sense

entries.meaning: In terms of sight or light; by means of light or lenses. ---
examples: The glass is optically clear, so it's used in camera lenses.
The disc is read optically by a laser.
Satellite images can be enlarged optically without losing detail.
entries.position: before its word — optically clear; end in the manner sense

entries.meaning: In the best or most effective way possible. ---
examples: The software helps the engine run optimally.
Plants grow optimally at about 75 degrees.
We need to use our budget optimally.

entries.meaning: Optimistically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She spoke optimistically about the company's future.
We optimistically packed shorts for the trip.
Optimistically, the repairs will take two weeks.
The house will be finished in March, optimistically.

senses.head: In a hopeful way, expecting things to go well
examples: She spoke optimistically about the company's future.
We optimistically packed shorts for the trip.

senses.head: In the best case — commenting on an estimate
body: (при самом лучшем раскладе, в лучшем случае)
examples: Optimistically, the repairs will take two weeks.
The house will be finished in March, optimistically.

entries.position: any position — end for manner; front as a comment (Optimistically, …)

entries.meaning: If you choose to; not as a requirement. ---
examples: The salad can optionally be topped with nuts.
Students may optionally submit a second essay.
Enter your email address and, optionally, a phone number.

entries.meaning: In a rich, expensive and showy way. ---
examples: The hotel lobby is opulently decorated in gold and marble.
They lived opulently in a mansion on Lake Michigan.
The guests arrived opulently dressed for the gala.
entries.position: before its word — opulently decorated; also end

entries.meaning: Or else has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Wear a jacket, or else you'll freeze.
We need to leave now, or else we'll miss the train.
You have to pay by Friday, or else you lose your spot.
Be home by midnight, or else!
You'd better return my car, or else.

senses.head: Otherwise; if not, then something bad will happen
examples: Wear a jacket, or else you'll freeze.
We need to leave now, or else we'll miss the train.
You have to pay by Friday, or else you lose your spot.

senses.head: Used alone at the end as a threat of punishment
examples: Be home by midnight, or else!
You'd better return my car, or else.

entries.русский: иначе, а то; а не то (пеняй на себя)
entries.position: front — of the second clause, after a comma; alone at the end as a threat
entries.contrast: It joins two clauses like a conjunction: Hurry up, or else we'll be late. Standing alone at the end (Pay up, or else!) it is an open threat, so avoid it in polite requests.

entries.meaning: Approximately; a little more or less than the amount given. ---
examples: I'll be there in twenty minutes or so.
The repair cost a hundred dollars or so.
There were fifty people or so at the party.
entries.position: after its word — right after a number or amount
entries.modifies: numbers and amounts of time, money, people
entries.contrast: About and around go before the number; or so goes after it: about ten minutes = ten minutes or so.

entries.meaning: Orally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The test will be given orally.
These stories were passed down orally for generations.
He agreed to the deal orally but never signed anything.
Take this medication orally with food.
The drug can be given orally or by injection.

senses.head: In speech rather than in writing
examples: The test will be given orally.
These stories were passed down orally for generations.
He agreed to the deal orally but never signed anything.

senses.head: By mouth — about medicine
examples: Take this medication orally with food.
The drug can be given orally or by injection.

entries.meaning: Usually; in normal circumstances. ---
examples: Ordinarily, I'd say no, but this is an emergency.
The drive ordinarily takes about an hour.
He doesn't ordinarily drink coffee this late.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb; also front (Ordinarily, …)

entries.meaning: Organically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: All our vegetables are organically grown.
The farm raises its chickens organically.
The business grew organically from a single food truck.
Their friendship developed organically over the years.

senses.head: Without artificial chemicals — about farming and food
examples: All our vegetables are organically grown.
The farm raises its chickens organically.

senses.head: Naturally and gradually, without being forced or planned
examples: The business grew organically from a single food truck.
Their friendship developed organically over the years.

entries.meaning: With a lot of detailed decoration. ---
examples: The ceiling was ornately painted with angels and clouds.
She wore an ornately embroidered silk jacket.
The old theater's lobby is ornately decorated in red and gold.
entries.position: before its word — usually a past participle (ornately carved)

entries.meaning: As it appears or is said to be, though perhaps not really. ---
examples: He left the meeting early, ostensibly to catch a flight.
The trip was ostensibly about trade, but everyone knew it was political.
Ostensibly, the new rule is meant to protect customers.
entries.type: stance — what is claimed, which may not be the real reason
entries.position: mid — or before the phrase it comments on; also front
entries.modifies: clauses and phrases, especially reasons (ostensibly to…)

entries.meaning: In a showy way meant to attract attention or impress people. ---
examples: He ostentatiously checked his gold watch.
Their house is ostentatiously decorated, with marble everywhere.
She yawned ostentatiously while he was talking.

entries.meaning: Out front has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I'll wait for you out front.
There's a taxi out front.
Park out front and come in.
She stayed out front for the whole race.
The company wants to be out front on new technology.

senses.head: Outside, in front of a building
examples: I'll wait for you out front.
There's a taxi out front.
Park out front and come in.

senses.head: In the leading position, ahead of the others
examples: She stayed out front for the whole race.
The company wants to be out front on new technology.

entries.meaning: In a voice others can hear, not silently. ---
examples: Read the sentence out loud.
I laughed out loud at his message.
Sorry, I was just thinking out loud.
entries.type: manner — so that others can hear
entries.modifies: verbs of reading, saying, laughing, thinking
entries.contrast: Out loud means audibly, not silently; it does not mean loudly. Aloud means the same and is more formal.

entries.meaning: Immediately and without serious thought, of rejecting something. ---
examples: The board rejected the proposal out of hand.
Don't dismiss the idea out of hand.
She refused his offer out of hand.
entries.contrast: Get out of hand (выйти из-под контроля) uses the same words as an adjective-like complement: The party got out of hand. After reject or dismiss it means immediately, without thinking about it.

entries.meaning: In a place where it cannot be seen. ---
examples: Keep your valuables out of sight in the car.
The plane climbed until it was out of sight.
Out of sight, out of mind.
entries.русский: вне поля зрения, с глаз долой
entries.type: place — where it cannot be seen

entries.meaning: Suddenly and without any warning. ---
examples: An old friend called me out of the blue.
Out of the blue, she announced she was moving to Texas.
The job offer came out of the blue.
entries.русский: ни с того ни с сего, как гром среди ясного неба

entries.meaning: Out of the way has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Get out of the way!
Could you move your car out of the way?
Keep the cables out of the way.
Let's get the paperwork out of the way first.
Once the exams are out of the way, we can relax.

senses.head: Not blocking someone's path
examples: Get out of the way!
Could you move your car out of the way?
Keep the cables out of the way.

senses.head: Finished, so it no longer needs attention
examples: Let's get the paperwork out of the way first.
Once the exams are out of the way, we can relax.

entries.contrast: Hyphenated before a noun it is an adjective meaning remote: an out-of-the-way village. Go out of your way means to make a special effort.

entries.meaning: From nowhere, as if by magic; with nothing to base it on. ---
examples: The deer seemed to appear out of thin air.
You can't just make up numbers out of thin air.
The money didn't come out of thin air.

entries.meaning: To parents who are not married to each other. ---
examples: He was born out of wedlock.
Having a baby out of wedlock is common now.
The share of children born out of wedlock has risen.
entries.position: end — usually right after born or have a child

entries.meaning: In a very strange or unusual way, often to a ridiculous degree. ---
examples: He showed up outlandishly dressed in a purple cape.
The prices at that resort are outlandishly high.
She decorated her apartment outlandishly, with neon signs on every wall.
entries.position: before its word — usually an adjective or participle (outlandishly dressed)

entries.meaning: Outrageously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Rents in this neighborhood are outrageously expensive.
The movie was outrageously funny.
Concert tickets have gotten outrageously overpriced.
The fans behaved outrageously after the game.
He flirted outrageously with everyone at the party.

senses.head: Extremely, to a shocking degree — often about prices, cost or humor
examples: Rents in this neighborhood are outrageously expensive.
The movie was outrageously funny.
Concert tickets have gotten outrageously overpriced.

senses.head: In a shocking or offensive way
examples: The fans behaved outrageously after the game.
He flirted outrageously with everyone at the party.

entries.position: before its word — or end when it describes behavior

entries.meaning: Outright has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The board rejected the plan outright.
She didn't lie outright, but she left out a lot.
He asked me outright whether I was quitting.
They bought the house outright, with no mortgage.
Two passengers were killed outright in the crash.

senses.head: Openly and completely, without holding anything back
examples: The board rejected the plan outright.
She didn't lie outright, but she left out a lot.
He asked me outright whether I was quitting.

senses.head: Fully and at once, not in parts or over time
examples: They bought the house outright, with no mortgage.
Two passengers were killed outright in the crash.

entries.type: manner — openly, completely, or at once
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.contrast: The adjective goes before a noun and is stressed on the first syllable: an outright lie (ˈaʊtraɪt), an outright ban. The adverb comes after the verb: They banned it outright.

entries.meaning: Extremely well or to an extremely high degree; far better than usual. ---
examples: The team played outstandingly well this season.
She was an outstandingly talented pianist.
The new vaccine has been outstandingly successful.

entries.meaning: On the surface; in the way someone or something appears. ---
examples: She stayed outwardly calm, but her hands were shaking.
Outwardly, the two brothers seemed to get along.
The building looks outwardly the same, but the inside is brand new.
entries.type: stance — how things look, as opposed to how they are
entries.modifies: adjectives (outwardly calm), verbs and whole clauses
entries.contrast: For direction (наружу) use outward: The door opens outward. Outwardly is about appearance: outwardly calm = внешне спокойный.

entries.meaning: Once more, from the beginning. ---
examples: I lost the file and had to write it all over again.
If I could live my life over again, I'd travel more.
Let's start over again.
entries.type: frequency — one more time, from the beginning
entries.contrast: Americans often drop again: Do it over, start over. In British English do it over can mean attack or redecorate.

entries.meaning: Many times, again and again. ---
examples: The kids watched the same movie over and over.
I've told you over and over again to lock the door.
She kept repeating his name over and over.
entries.type: frequency — many times in a row

entries.meaning: In or to this place, close to the speaker. ---
examples: Come over here and look at this.
Your keys are over here on the table.
Hey, we're over here!
entries.contrast: Over here and over there point to a spot the listener should look at; plain here is less pointed. Over does not mean above here.

entries.meaning: Too; more than is reasonable or necessary. ---
examples: Don't be overly critical of yourself.
The instructions were overly complicated.
I'm not overly worried about the test.
entries.contrast: Overly is especially common in American English; British English often uses the prefix instead (over-cautious). Not overly is a polite understatement: I'm not overly worried = я не особенно волнуюсь.

entries.meaning: So strongly that it overwhelms you. ---
examples: The room smelled overpoweringly of cheap perfume.
The sauce was overpoweringly salty.
It was overpoweringly hot inside the car.
entries.type: degree — so strongly that it is hard to bear
entries.position: before its word — or after a verb like smell
entries.modifies: adjectives and verbs of sense (smell, taste)

entries.meaning: Beyond the usual hours of work. ---
examples: The nurses worked overtime all week.
He's been working overtime to pay off his student loans.
Her imagination was working overtime after the scary movie.
entries.type: duration — beyond the regular working hours
entries.contrast: Also a noun: get paid overtime (сверхурочные), The game went into overtime (дополнительное время). Work overtime is the adverb, and working overtime is also used figuratively for something very busy.

entries.meaning: Openly, in a way that is not hidden. ---
examples: The ad isn't overtly political, but the message is clear.
He never overtly threatened anyone.
Some voters were overtly hostile to the idea.

entries.meaning: To a very great degree; by a very large majority.
examples: The bill passed overwhelmingly.
Voters are overwhelmingly in favor of the new park.
The reviews have been overwhelmingly positive.
entries.position: before its word — or end (passed overwhelmingly)
